source.title: LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in Large Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The study compares performance on an in-context interference task across model sizes, a different measure and task from pretraining-loss scaling, and reports whether performance predicts with size.
record.gate_note: The study measures interference-task accuracy and endurance, not held-out cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal allocations. Only results bearing on downstream-task predictability with scale (V6) are recorded. The individual model scores in Table 4 are not separately extracted; the reported cross-model regression and group comparisons summarize the scale-performance results.
record.test_reason: The study regresses endurance scores on two in-context interference tasks (RI, PI) against parameter count across 39 LLMs. That is a new downstream setting with a result on whether performance improves with scale (V6). It measures no pretraining loss, fits no power law and does no compute allocation, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested. T3 fits better than T2: the scale comparison is a cross-sectional set of heterogeneous commercial and open models, not a method aimed at the scaling question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' central conclusions are that every model shows PI more damaging than RI (39/39, d=1.73), the reverse of humans, and that four lines of evidence indicate distinct RI and PI mechanisms. Those lines are: scale predicts RI but not PI; RI and PI correlate weakly; error profiles differ; and RI decays smoothly while PI collapses bimodally. They attribute this to a primacy bias in transformer attention and caution that the results come from a single paradigm.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an AB-AC paired-associate interference evaluation and relates endurance scores to model size; it does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws for parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size association differs by interference condition: it is significant for RI and not significant for PI. The study also reports different RIES associations when using dense-only, total, or estimated active parameter counts.
record.problems: The study uses a single AB-AC paradigm and English-only stimuli, tests only transformer architectures, and reports complete paired RI–PI analyses on 39 models. It states that proprietary parameter counts are estimates and that mechanistic accounts are post-hoc and unconfirmed by attention probing.
record.rows_left_out: The individual RIES and PIES values for all models in Table 4 are not separately extracted; the cross-model regression results and reported size-tier comparison are recorded instead.

untested.parts: No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or regime with loss scaling.
Predictability from pretraining loss. Whether improvement follows a predictable functional form, as opposed to a positive correlation. Other downstream tasks.
No exponent fitting or fitting-choice sensitivity of loss laws.

missing.what: PI decay curves by size tier are non-monotonic: the M tier outperforms the L tier.
Per-model RIES/PIES by parameter count, needed to judge the reliability of the size axis (e.g. GPT-5-nano listed at 2500B with PIES 21.0).

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The scale evidence is cross-sectional over heterogeneous models with estimated proprietary sizes, and it confounds size with model family, training and reasoning mode (reasoning models score higher on RI, Section 4.3). Treat the V6 support as weak. The cited Wang and Sun R2=0.26 for PI is a cited result and should not be a row.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests performance on one controlled in-context interference task against model size. It does not test other downstream tasks or whether performance predicts from pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of loss-scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations to fitting choices, and departures of loss curves from a power law.

rows.subject: 39 LLMs with complete paired RI–PI data
rows.operation_detail: Regressed Retroactive Interference Endurance Score (RIES) on parameter count across models.
rows.measure: Association of parameter count with RIES
rows.note: The authors report a positive association between model size and resistance to RI.
rows.check: Linear regression on total parameter count across heterogeneous models (different data, training, MoE/dense). It is unclear whether the axis is linear or log. Proprietary sizes are estimates, e.g. GPT-5, -mini and -nano are all listed at 2500B. The state is fine, but it is a correlation, not a fitted scaling law.

rows.subject: 39 LLMs with complete paired RI–PI data
rows.operation_detail: Regressed Proactive Interference Endurance Score (PIES) on parameter count across models.
rows.measure: Association of parameter count with PIES
rows.note: The authors explicitly state that size does not predict PI resistance in this sample.
rows.check: Correct. Fig. 4 also shows the M tier outperforming the larger L tier on PI, which the row could note.

rows.subject: 39 LLMs with complete paired RI–PI data
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean RIES across parameter-count tiers.
rows.value: 171.2 for the largest tier (>500B); a 28-point gap
rows.note: The reported tier comparison supports higher RI resistance in the largest size group.
rows.check: OK. The F-test is across four tiers, not only the two compared.

rows.subject: 39 LLMs with complete paired RI–PI data
rows.operation_detail: Re-estimated the parameter-count association with RIES using dense-only parameters.
rows.measure: Association of parameter count with RIES
rows.note: Reported as a robustness analysis of the positive size–RI relationship.
rows.check: Robustness variant of R1. Same subject and confounds.

rows.subject: 39 LLMs with complete paired RI–PI data
rows.operation_detail: Measured the parameter-count association with RIES using total parameters.
rows.measure: Association of parameter count with RIES
rows.note: The total-parameter result is reported alongside the dense-only and estimated-active-parameter analyses.
rows.check: Duplicates R1: same total-parameter regression (R2=0.49), restated in the robustness sentence. Should be merged with R1.

rows.subject: 39 LLMs with complete paired RI–PI data
rows.operation_detail: Re-estimated the parameter-count association with RIES using estimated active parameters.
rows.measure: Association of parameter count with RIES
rows.note: The association remains positive using estimated active parameters, though the reported R2 is smaller.
rows.check: With estimated active parameters R2 drops to 0.30, a clearly weaker association than total or dense counts. The active counts are the authors' estimates.

relationships.condition: Retroactive-interference endurance (RIES) across 39 LLMs, total or dense parameter counts
relationships.reason: RIES rises with parameter count (R2≈0.49–0.54) and the largest tier beats the smallest by 28 points (R1, R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Interference endurance increased with model size at R²≈0.49–0.54, and the largest tier exceeded the smallest by 28 points.

relationships.condition: Proactive-interference endurance (PIES); RIES with estimated active parameters
relationships.reason: Size does not predict PIES (R2=0.06, n.s.), and the RI association weakens to R2=0.30 with active parameters, so it depends on task and parameter counting (R2, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Size did not significantly predict proactive-interference endurance (R²=0.06), while the retroactive-interference association weakened to R²=0.30 when using estimated active parameters.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
